what_it_does: When large scientific or AI programs are built by combining several libraries, each library independently runs its own GPU operations (self-contained programs called 'kernels' that execute on the graphics chip) and moves its own data in and out of memory, unaware of what the other libraries are doing. This means the same data is often copied multiple times unnecessarily, and each kernel launch has overhead costs that add up. Diffuse is a system that watches across all these libraries simultaneously by representing every library's computation in a shared intermediate form (a common language for describing work to be done). Using this shared representation, a just-in-time compiler (one that translates and optimizes code on the fly as the program runs) can identify when two separate pieces of work from different libraries can be merged into one combined operation, eliminating redundant data transfers and kernel launch costs without requiring programmers to modify their application code.
